intro: Scriabin’s Piano Sonata No. 5, Op. 53, is in a single movement marked Allegro impetuoso con stravaganza. A low rumble rises to the top of the piano and a quiet, languid reply follows; the soft opening song builds to a triple-forte climax.

cues.title: Opening, Presto and Languido
cues.text: A trill and a rumbling left hand send a rush of notes upwards. After a pause comes Languido, with soft chords and a melody marked con voglia, “with desire”.
cues.evidence: Author’s edition, engraved by C. G. Röder, pp. 2–3: Allegro impetuoso con stravaganza, Presto, a fermata, then Languido, pp dolcissimo and con voglia. https://hdl.handle.net/1802/30620
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Main theme, Presto con allegrezza
cues.text: Presto con allegrezza (very fast, with joy) marks the sonata’s main theme. The right-hand chords fall against the left hand’s leaping accompaniment, so that the phrase is syncopated across the beat.
cues.evidence: Author’s edition, p. 4, the Presto con allegrezza theme. Gerald Larner identifies its syncopation and its role as the main subject. https://hdl.handle.net/1802/30620; https://geraldlarner.com/work/scriabin-piano-sonata-no-5-in-f-sharp-major-op-53-1907
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Meno vivo theme
cues.text: The slower Meno vivo brings another melody, marked accarezzevole (caressingly), over chromatic inner voices. In the development this theme returns louder and more forceful.
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner describes the Meno vivo theme, its accarezzevole marking, chromatic counterpoint and climactic treatment in the development. https://geraldlarner.com/work/scriabin-piano-sonata-no-5-in-f-sharp-major-op-53-1907
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Single-movement form, 1907
cues.text: Scriabin wrote the Fifth in 1907. It was the first of his numbered piano sonatas in a single movement, and he kept that form for all five that followed. Its slow, fast and ecstatic passages make up one continuous span.
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner gives the date, one-movement form and its continuation in Sonatas Nos. 6–10. The preceding four sonatas have more than one movement; the Fifth is identified as the first single-movement sonata in the work history. https://geraldlarner.com/work/scriabin-piano-sonata-no-5-in-f-sharp-major-op-53-1907; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Sonata_No._5_(Scriabin)

cues.title: Scriabin’s epigraph
cues.text: Above the first bar Scriabin printed lines from his own Poem of Ecstasy, in French and Russian. The first reads: “I call you to life, O mysterious forces!” The next three lines call up timid beginnings of life from the dark depths of the creative spirit.
cues.evidence: Author’s edition, p. 2, prints the epigraph in French and Russian. The quoted first line translates “Je vous appelle à la vie, ô forces mystérieuses!”; the remaining description follows the next three lines. https://hdl.handle.net/1802/30620

cues.title: Recapitulation and return of the Presto
cues.text: After the climax of the development, the skipping Presto returns and the themes of the exposition are recapitulated. The quiet con voglia theme from the introduction is then expanded.
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner describes the development’s climax, the recapitulation of the exposition’s themes, and the subsequent enlargement of the introductory con voglia theme. https://geraldlarner.com/work/scriabin-piano-sonata-no-5-in-f-sharp-major-op-53-1907
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Climax in E♭ major, estatico
cues.text: The soft introductory song returns estatico and triple forte, high above repeated chords. The harmony is E♭ major, while the sonata’s home key is F♯. On the last page the introductory rushing figure returns, rising, and the piece ends on a rest with no final chord.
cues.evidence: Author’s edition, p. 19: estatico, fff, E-flat-major harmony, then the introductory rushing figure and a final rest. Gerald Larner describes the displaced tonal climax and unanchored ending. https://hdl.handle.net/1802/30620; https://geraldlarner.com/work/scriabin-piano-sonata-no-5-in-f-sharp-major-op-53-1907
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: Composer who wrote a part for coloured light that had to be omitted at the work’s first performance.
facts: Moscow Conservatory, 1888–92: Safonov, Taneyev and Arensky
Piano professor at the Moscow Conservatory from 1898
Publisher Mitrofan Belyayev; conductor Serge Koussevitzky
Ten piano sonatas; three symphonies; a concerto; The Poem of Ecstasy and Prometheus
composer.background:
At the Moscow première of Prometheus in 1911, Scriabin sat at the piano and Serge Koussevitzky conducted. The audience heard the large orchestra, the solo piano and the sustained harmonies that precede the first horn melody. One part of the score was not performed: the keyboard intended to project coloured light. Alexander Mozer had built a small apparatus for Scriabin, but because of technical difficulties Scriabin withdrew it from the concert, and the première went ahead without the lights.

He was born in Moscow in 1872. His mother, Lyubov, was a trained pianist; she died when he was a baby. His father was pursuing a diplomatic career abroad, and his aunt, also Lyubov, helped bring him up. He entered the cadet corps in 1882, took lessons from Nikolai Zverev, and joined Vasily Safonov’s piano class at the Moscow Conservatory in 1888. Rachmaninoff studied there too. Scriabin graduated as a pianist in 1892, a year after Rachmaninoff, but left without completing the composition course with Sergei Taneyev and Anton Arensky.
